av.title: A global promise
av.text: MetLife has been a trusted source of financial security since 1868. Today it serves customers in more than forty markets, from group benefits for most of the Fortune 500 to retirement income, asset management, and fast-growing markets like Mexico, Brazil and India.

av.title: The New Frontier
av.text: Under its New Frontier strategy, MetLife is committed to double-digit earnings growth, fifteen to seventeen percent return on equity, a one hundred basis point lower direct expense ratio, and more than twenty five billion dollars of free cash flow. Every one of those commitments runs on technology.

av.title: The era of network operations is changing
av.text: For decades, operations meant separate tools for network, cloud, applications and security, with alerts that arrive after customers are already affected. Each team sees a slice. Nobody sees the business.

av.title: One fabric of data
av.text: The Cisco Data Fabric, powered by Splunk, brings machine data from every domain, including network, internet, cloud, applications, identity and security, together with business events and external signals like weather and market calendars, into one federated, AI-ready picture.

av.title: A vantage point above it all
av.text: Cisco Cloud Control is the unified control plane for AgenticOps. Governed AI agents watch that picture continuously. They correlate weak signals across domains, forecast business impact, and propose or take action under policy, with humans approving in AI Canvas.

av.title: From IT problems to business outcomes
av.text: In the ten missions ahead, each one at a real MetLife location, you will watch the same moment play out twice: once the traditional way, and once with AgenticOps. Use the timeline to move through time, make the call at each decision point, and see the business value protected.

ov: Ten locations, ten business moments, and one pattern. In every mission the signal was there hours or days before the business would have felt it. What changed the outcome was a vantage point above every domain: the Cisco Data Fabric bringing the data together, and governed agents in Cisco Cloud Control acting under policy with people in control. That is how operations moves from fixing IT problems to protecting revenue, customers, compliance and cost. It is how technology helps MetLife deliver on the New Frontier.

lv.title: Open Enrollment Surge
lv.subtitle: New York | Group Benefits
lv.industryChallenge: Open enrollment compresses a year of employee benefit decisions into a few weeks. Portal slowdowns turn into employer escalations, service-level credits and renewal risk.
lv.exposureBasis: Modeled: about 6 hours of degraded enrollment across large employer clients, plus service-level credits, surge contact-center cost and renewal risk on a small slice of group premium.

events.text: Built a traffic model from the last three enrollment seasons. Forecast peak: 3.1x normal at the opening bell.
Synthetic logins show p95 latency up 38% under rehearsal load. The forecast breaches the SLO at T-0.
Found a shared bottleneck: the auth token service plus WAN egress at the North Greenbush, New York data center.
Plan drafted: scale the auth tier, pre-warm the CDN, shift 30% of traffic to the secondary region. Policy check passed. Approved by an operator.
Changes executed. Synthetic tests confirm 2.4x headroom.
Enrollment opens. Peak absorbed. Login p95 stays under 1.2s.
The same signals exist across four tools. Nobody correlates them.
Enrollment opens. Login takes 9 seconds and sessions time out.
Ticket volume spikes 11x. A P1 bridge opens with six teams.
Root cause found after the fact: auth tier and egress saturation.
Service restored. Employer escalations and SLA credit requests follow.

narration.overview: Mission one, New York. MetLife is the number one group benefits provider in the United States and serves more than eighty five percent of the Fortune 500. Open enrollment is when that leadership is tested in public. In this mission, the Cisco Data Fabric learns from past enrollment seasons, and agents in Cisco Cloud Control spot a capacity bottleneck two days before the portal opens. Instead of a war room and employer escalations, the busiest hour of the year looks like any other hour.
narration.briefing: We are at MetLife headquarters in New York. Millions of employees at client companies are about to choose their benefits in a narrow window. Every minute of a slow or failing portal shows up in an employer relationship, and those relationships drive group benefits revenue.
narration.signal: Forty eight hours before enrollment opens, the capacity agent runs a rehearsal using ThousandEyes synthetic logins. Login latency is creeping up. On its own that looks like noise. But the Data Fabric correlates it with identity logs and WAN egress telemetry from the MetLife data center in North Greenbush, New York, and the forecast says the service level breaks the moment enrollment opens.
narration.traditional: Here is the traditional path. Each tool held part of the story, but nobody connected the pieces. Enrollment opens, logins time out, the service desk is flooded, and six teams spend hours on a bridge call finding a root cause that was visible two days earlier. The employers notice first.
narration.agentic: Here is the AgenticOps path. The agent drafts a remediation plan in AI Canvas: scale the authentication tier, pre-warm the content delivery network, and shift part of the traffic to the secondary region. The plan is checked against change policy, an operator approves it, and synthetic tests confirm there is headroom. When enrollment opens, the peak is absorbed.
narration.outcome: The business outcome is not a faster ticket. It is a clean open enrollment, protected employer relationships, and group benefits revenue that is never put at risk. That is the conversation to have with the head of group benefits, not just with the network team.

decision.prompt: The capacity agent forecasts an SLO breach at the opening bell, 48 hours out. What do you do?

options.label: Approve the agent plan in AI Canvas
options.detail: Policy-checked scaling and traffic shift, verified by synthetic tests.
options.feedback: Correct. A governed agent acts early with a human approval. The peak is absorbed and the business never sees it.

options.label: Open a ticket for the capacity team
options.detail: Route it through the normal change queue for next week.
options.feedback: The ticket is still in the queue when enrollment opens. You get partial relief, but the opening hour is still degraded.

options.label: Wait and watch
options.detail: Latency is still within SLO today.
options.feedback: The signal was real. Enrollment opens into a degraded portal and a six-team war room.

chain.signal: Synthetic login latency creeping up under rehearsal load
chain.domain: Identity, application and WAN, correlated in the Data Fabric
chain.capability: Capacity agent with a policy-governed change in Cisco Cloud Control
chain.kpi: Enrollment completion rate and employer satisfaction
chain.outcome: Group Benefits revenue and renewals protected

talkTrack: Open enrollment is a revenue event, not an IT event. Start the conversation with the group benefits leaders.
The value is in correlation. ThousandEyes, application traces and identity logs each look fine alone. Together they predict the failure.
Agents act under policy with a human approval in AI Canvas. That answers the control question before it is asked.

options: Data Fabric correlation of synthetic tests, identity and WAN telemetry with past seasons

lv.title: The Change That Never Broke
lv.subtitle: Cary, NC | Global Technology
lv.industryChallenge: Most major outages in financial services start with a change. Large insurers run thousands of changes a month across hybrid data centers and clouds, and manual reviews cannot see every dependency.
lv.exposureBasis: Modeled: about 4 hours of core platform outage at roughly $40K per minute, a common downtime benchmark for top-tier financial services firms.

events.text: Saturday 02:00 change ingested: fabric firmware upgrade plus an ACL update on the leaf pair serving the policy admin cluster.
Pre-change analysis: the new ACL plus existing config drift on leaf-14 would block the database replication path.
Blast radius: 41 applications, including claims intake, the agent portal and Japan batch jobs.
Corrected ACL and drift remediation proposed. Change owner and CAB approve the revision.
Revised change verified in the digital twin. Risk score drops from 92 to 11.
Change window: executed clean. Post-change assurance passed.
Change approved on a spreadsheet review. The drift on leaf-14 is unknown.
Replication path blocked. Core policy platform goes down globally.
Hundreds of alarms from 12 tools. Rollback attempted and it fails.
Drift found by hand. ACL fixed.
Recovered. Weekend claims and batch backlogs need overtime to clear.

narration.overview: Mission two, the global technology campus in Cary, North Carolina. Most major outages begin with a change. Here, a routine weekend firmware and access list change would have collided with undocumented configuration drift and taken down the core policy platform worldwide. The change agent in Cisco Cloud Control models the change against the real network before it runs, finds the collision, and proposes a corrected change. The outage never happens, and neither does the overtime.
narration.briefing: We are at the MetLife Global Technology Campus in Cary, North Carolina: three seven-story buildings above Lake Crabtree, home to the engineers who build and run MetLife platforms. Their changes land in hybrid infrastructure, including the MetLife data center in North Greenbush, New York, and cloud regions that support claims, policy administration and partner systems around the world. A single change can touch dozens of business services.
narration.signal: Twenty hours before the change window, the agent pulls the change record, the Nexus Dashboard intent model and the latest configuration snapshots into the Data Fabric. It finds that the new access list, combined with drift on one leaf switch, would block database replication for the policy administration cluster. It maps the blast radius: forty one applications.
narration.traditional: In the traditional path, the change board approves the change from a spreadsheet. Nobody knows about the drift. At two in the morning, replication stops and the policy platform goes down globally. Twelve tools raise hundreds of alarms, the rollback fails, and it takes hours to find the cause by hand.
narration.agentic: In the AgenticOps path, the agent presents its evidence in AI Canvas, along with a corrected access list and a drift fix. The change owner and the change board approve the revision. It is verified in a digital twin, the risk score drops from ninety two to eleven, and the change runs clean.
narration.outcome: This mission is about operating efficiency, which maps directly to the New Frontier commitment to lower the direct expense ratio by one hundred basis points. Fewer failed changes means fewer war rooms, less overtime, and engineers who spend their weekends building rather than recovering.

decision.prompt: The change agent rates the Saturday change at risk 92 because of a hidden drift collision. What do you do?

options.label: Accept the agent-corrected change
options.detail: Fix the drift, revise the ACL, verify in the digital twin.
options.feedback: Correct. The change runs clean on schedule with no outage and no overtime.

options.label: Postpone the change a month
options.detail: Avoid risk by doing nothing.
options.feedback: The outage is avoided, but the firmware security fix slips and the drift stays in the network.

options.label: Proceed as approved
options.detail: CAB already signed off.
options.feedback: The collision happens and the core policy platform goes down for hours.

chain.signal: A change record that conflicts with existing config drift
chain.domain: Data center fabric, application dependencies and change management
chain.capability: Pre-change verification and blast-radius mapping by a governed agent
chain.kpi: Change failure rate and core platform availability
chain.outcome: Lower direct expense ratio and a resilient policy platform

talkTrack: Tie change risk to the direct expense ratio commitment. Every avoided war room is real cost.
The agent does not replace the change board. It gives the board evidence it never had.
Blast radius is the language of business owners: 41 applications, not one switch.
discovery: What share of your major incidents last year started with a change?
How does your change board see configuration drift today?
How long does it take to map which business services depend on a given switch or cluster?

quiz.q: Which New Frontier commitment does this mission support most directly?
options: 100 basis point reduction in direct expense ratio
quiz.why: Avoided outages and recovery effort lower operating cost.

quiz.q: What made the change risky?
options: An ACL combined with undocumented drift
quiz.why: Pre-change analysis against the real network state revealed the collision.

lv.title: Ahead of the Storm
lv.subtitle: Tampa, FL | Claims and Customer Care
lv.industryChallenge: Catastrophes hit insurers twice: the event itself and the surge of claims and calls that follows. That surge often lands just as local sites lose power, carriers or staff.
lv.exposureBasis: Modeled: two days of reduced claims and care capacity during a catastrophe surge, including call abandonment, claim cycle-time penalties, overtime and reputational impact.

events.text: External signal joined: hurricane cone now covers Tampa Bay. Landfall forecast in about 84 hours.
Risk found: two of three carrier circuits share a flood-zone central office. The forecast claims surge is 6x.
Playbook: activate 5G SD-WAN backup, pre-shift 40% of voice routing to Noida and remote agents, scale claims intake.
Storm IVR and callback queues published. Remote agent headsets verified via Meraki.
Failover rehearsed. Tampa can lose both shared circuits with no customer impact.
Landfall: two circuits drop. Traffic is already on 5G and the alternate carrier. Claims intake keeps up.
Storm prep focuses on buildings. Circuit diversity is assumed.
Landfall: both shared circuits fail. Contact center voice goes down.
Call abandonment hits 48% as claims calls surge 6x.
Manual reroute to other sites. Agents are not provisioned yet.
Capacity restored. Claim backlog and regulator inquiries follow.

narration.overview: Mission three, Tampa. When a hurricane hits, MetLife customers need their insurer most, and that is exactly when local sites can lose carriers and power. In this mission, the resilience agent joins a public storm track with network and contact center telemetry three days before landfall. It finds that two carrier circuits share a flood zone, pre-stages failover, and moves voice capacity ahead of time. When the storm arrives, customers reach a person and claims keep moving.
narration.briefing: Tampa is a major claims and customer care hub. Customers in a disaster need fast claim intake and a human voice. Service level here is not just a metric. It is the moment MetLife keeps its promise.
narration.signal: Seventy two hours before landfall, the Data Fabric brings in the storm track and lines it up with the network. The agent finds that two of the three carrier circuits run through the same central office inside the flood zone. It also forecasts a six-fold surge in claims calls.
narration.traditional: In the traditional path, storm preparation focuses on buildings and generators. Circuit diversity is assumed. At landfall both shared circuits fail and contact center voice goes down. Nearly half of the callers hang up, and it takes more than a day to reroute and provision agents elsewhere.
narration.agentic: In the AgenticOps path, the agent proposes a playbook in AI Canvas. It activates 5G backup on SD-WAN, pre-shifts forty percent of voice routing to the Noida operations center and to remote agents, publishes storm call flows in Webex Contact Center, and rehearses the failover. At landfall, two circuits drop and nobody calling in notices.
narration.outcome: This is business resiliency made visible. Claims are paid quickly, care stays reachable, and regulators see an insurer that was ready. Resilience is easy to promise in a policy document. This shows how it actually gets delivered.

decision.prompt: Landfall is 72 hours out, and two of the three circuits share a flood-zone central office. What do you do?

options.label: Run the agent resilience playbook
options.detail: 5G SD-WAN backup, pre-shift voice, scale claims intake, rehearse failover.
options.feedback: Correct. Landfall becomes a non-event for customers and claims stay ahead of the surge.

options.label: Order a new diverse circuit
options.detail: Carrier lead time is about 45 days.
options.feedback: Good long-term fix, but it will not arrive before this storm.

options.label: Rely on the existing DR plan
options.detail: The plan was tested last year.
options.feedback: The plan assumed circuit diversity that does not exist. Voice goes down at landfall.

chain.signal: Storm track combined with shared-path circuit risk
chain.domain: SD-WAN, carriers, contact center and claims systems
chain.capability: Resilience agent with a pre-staged failover and capacity playbook
chain.kpi: Call abandonment and claim cycle time
chain.outcome: Customer trust and regulatory standing in a crisis

talkTrack: Put resilience in customer terms: can a policyholder reach a person after a disaster?
External data, like weather, joined with internal telemetry is a key strength of the Data Fabric.
Agents rehearse failover, so resilience is proven before the storm rather than hoped for during it.
discovery: How do you validate true path diversity for critical sites today?
In your last catastrophe event, how quickly could you shift contact center capacity?
Which external signals, like weather or carrier status, are part of your operations picture now?

options: Two circuits sharing a flood-zone central office
quiz.why: Shared-path risk is invisible without correlating carrier data with the physical world.

quiz.q: What business outcome leads this story?
options: Policyholders reach a person and claims keep moving
quiz.why: The claims promise is the brand promise.

lv.title: The Agent in the Living Room
lv.subtitle: Tokyo | MetLife Japan Retail and Annuities
lv.pillar: Capitalize on the retirement platform (U.S., U.K. and Japan)
lv.industryChallenge: In Japan, face-to-face sales channels remain critical. When a sales professional's tablet stalls in a customer's home, the sale and the trust stall with it. Earthquake readiness is also a constant requirement.
lv.exposureBasis: Modeled: a business day of degraded field sales, with lost or delayed annuity and life applications across face-to-face channels.

events.text: Packet loss is rising on one consumer ISP path toward the sales app gateway in the Osaka region.
Correlated: 18% of field tablets on that ISP show slow e-signature steps. Monday is a quarter-end sales push.
Plan: steer the sales app through an alternate Secure Access edge, open an ISP case with evidence, and pre-cache forms.
Path change verified. E-signature step time back to baseline.
Seismic drill check: DR region verified, and the field app can fail over in under 60 seconds.
Quarter-end push: application submissions 12% above plan.
A few complaints that the app is slow, logged as individual device issues.
Quarter-end push: e-signature fails in customer homes. Appointments end without a sale.
Regional managers escalate. IT suspects the app release.
The ISP issue is finally isolated after the app is rolled back.
Recovered. Lost appointments cannot be rescheduled before quarter close.

narration.overview: Mission four, Tokyo. Japan is MetLife's largest operation in Asia, and face-to-face sales are at the heart of it. A sales professional with a tablet in a customer's living room is MetLife's storefront. In this mission, ThousandEyes and real user monitoring pick up a degraded internet provider path a day before a quarter-end sales push. The agent steers traffic around it, so every appointment can end with a signed application.
narration.briefing: Tokyo anchors retail life and annuity sales in Japan, one of the three core retirement markets in MetLife's New Frontier strategy. Here the network extends into customers' homes over consumer internet connections that IT does not own.
narration.signal: Twenty six hours before the quarter-end push, the experience agent sees packet loss on one consumer provider path. It correlates that with real user monitoring from the sales app and finds that eighteen percent of field tablets are hitting slow e-signature steps. Individually these look like device complaints. Together they are a revenue risk.
narration.traditional: In the traditional path, each complaint is logged as a single device issue. On the big day, e-signatures fail in customers' homes. IT suspects the latest app release and rolls it back, which does not help. Hours later the internet provider is identified as the cause, but those appointments are gone.
narration.agentic: In the AgenticOps path, the agent proposes steering the sales app through an alternate Secure Access edge, pre-caching forms, and opening a provider case with ThousandEyes evidence. Once approved, the path change is verified within minutes. The resilience agent also checks earthquake failover readiness, because in Japan that is part of every day.
narration.outcome: The outcome is revenue and trust in the moments that matter most. Agents close more applications, customers have a smooth experience, and leadership sees technology working for the sales force. These are internet paths MetLife does not own, and they are still visible and manageable.

decision.prompt: The experience agent links a consumer ISP problem to slow e-signatures on 18% of field tablets the day before quarter-end. What do you do?

options.label: Approve the steering and pre-cache plan
options.detail: Alternate Secure Access edge, forms cached, ISP case opened with evidence.
options.feedback: Correct. Field sales run at full speed and the quarter closes above plan.

options.label: Tell the sales force to use hotspots
options.detail: Send a memo to 1,000s of agents.
options.feedback: Some appointments are saved. Many agents never see the memo, and customers notice the fumbling.

options.label: Roll back the latest app release
options.detail: The release is the usual suspect.
options.feedback: Wrong root cause. The problem continues and the team loses a day.

chain.domain: Internet paths, secure edge, mobile app and devices

chain.outcome: Retail and annuity revenue in a core retirement market

options: Failed e-signatures in customer homes mean lost sales
quiz.why: Face-to-face sales are critical in Japan, and the appointment is the sale.

lv.title: The Silent Conversion Leak
lv.subtitle: Mexico City | MetLife Xcelerator Partners
lv.industryChallenge: Embedded insurance sold through digital banks, e-wallets and retailers depends on APIs. When quote latency creeps up, partners quietly hide the offer, and nobody calls to complain.
lv.exposureBasis: Modeled: several days of lower conversion on embedded-insurance partner traffic, plus partner placement penalties on checkout pages.

events.text: Joined business events (quote, bind) with API traces for the top 20 partners.
Quote API p99 for one e-wallet partner rose from 380 ms to 1.9 s. Their checkout times out at 2 s, and conversion is starting to slip.
Root cause: DNS resolution in a new cloud region plus a cold cache on the rating service.
Plan: pin the resolver, warm the rating cache, add a latency SLO alert tied to partner contract terms.
p99 back to 410 ms. Partner conversion recovers before the weekend promotion.
Weekend promotion: binds are 22% above forecast.
All APIs return HTTP 200. The dashboards are green.
Weekend promotion: the partner checkout times out and quietly drops the insurance offer.
The partner asks why sales fell. IT sees no outage.
Latency root cause found after a manual trace review.
Fixed. The promotion window is gone and placement is under review.

narration.overview: Mission five, Mexico City. MetLife Xcelerator connects people with insurance through digital banks, e-wallets, e-commerce platforms and retailers. Those partnerships run on APIs, and APIs fail quietly. In this mission, the revenue agent links business events with API traces and sees that a partner's checkout is about to time out on MetLife's quote, even though every dashboard is green. It fixes the cause before a weekend promotion, and conversion grows instead of leaking away.
narration.briefing: Mexico is MetLife's largest market in Latin America, and high-growth international markets are a core New Frontier priority. Here growth is driven by digital partner distribution, where the customer never visits MetLife at all.
narration.signal: Forty hours before a partner's weekend promotion, the revenue agent sees quote latency for one e-wallet partner rise from under four hundred milliseconds to almost two seconds. That partner's checkout gives up at two seconds. The API is still returning success codes, so traditional monitoring is green. The business events tell a different story: conversion is starting to slip.
narration.traditional: In the traditional path, the dashboards stay green. During the promotion, the partner's checkout silently drops the insurance offer. Nobody raises an incident, because nothing is technically down. The first signal is a partner manager asking why sales fell, almost a day later.
narration.agentic: In the AgenticOps path, the correlation agent traces the latency to name resolution in a new cloud region and a cold cache on the rating service. It proposes pinning the resolver, warming the cache, and adding a service level alert tied to the partner contract. Latency recovers before the promotion begins.
narration.outcome: This is how observability becomes revenue intelligence. The agent watches business outcomes, not just uptime. MetLife keeps its place on partner checkout pages, which is how embedded insurance grows in high-growth markets.

decision.prompt: All APIs return success, but partner quote latency is close to the partner's checkout timeout. What do you do?

options.label: Let the revenue agent fix it and add a contract-tied SLO
options.detail: Pin the resolver, warm the cache, alert on partner terms.
options.feedback: Correct. Conversion recovers and the promotion outperforms.

options.label: Raise the alert threshold
options.detail: Reduce noise. Nothing is down.
options.feedback: The leak continues unseen through the promotion.

options.label: Ask the partner to extend their timeout
options.detail: Open a partner negotiation.
options.feedback: The partner may agree next quarter, but this weekend's revenue still leaks.

chain.signal: API latency approaching a partner timeout while returning success codes
chain.domain: Cloud, DNS, APIs and business events
chain.capability: Revenue agent correlating traces with quote and bind events

talkTrack: Green dashboards can hide red revenue. Combining business events with telemetry is what makes the difference.
Talk to the digital distribution leader about partner placement and conversion, not about latency.
Contract-aware service levels show IT understands how the business actually makes money.
discovery: How do you learn about partner API problems today: from monitoring or from the partner?
Are partner contract terms, like timeouts, reflected in your alerting?
Can you see conversion and latency on the same screen?

quiz.q: Why did traditional monitoring miss this?
options: The API was returning success codes while getting slower
quiz.why: Latency close to a partner timeout is invisible to up-or-down checks.

quiz.q: Who is the best executive audience for this story?
options: Head of digital distribution and partnerships
quiz.why: Partner conversion is their number.

lv.title: Pension Day
lv.subtitle: Santiago | Pensions and Annuities
lv.industryChallenge: Pension payments and regulatory reports have hard deadlines. A batch overrun means retirees paid late, regulators asking questions, and expensive manual fixes.
lv.exposureBasis: Modeled: late payment remediation, regulatory reporting penalties, manual reprocessing and service costs for a monthly pension cycle.

events.text: Learned normal run times for the monthly pension batch chain, 22 jobs.
Rehearsal shows job 14 running 2.7x slower. Forecast: bank file misses the cutoff by 3 hours.
Cause: a storage tier rebalance overlaps the batch window, and indexes have grown 30% on retiree records.
Plan: reschedule the rebalance, rebuild indexes, add parallel lanes to job 14. Operations approves.
Forecast now finishes 2 hours ahead of the bank cutoff.
Pension Day: every payment file delivered on time, and the regulatory report filed.
Jobs are green. Run times are not compared to history.
The bank cutoff is missed. Retiree payments are delayed.
Retirees call about missing payments.
The regulatory report is late. The regulator requests an explanation.
Payments released. Remediation and a formal response are required.

narration.overview: Mission six, Santiago. Pension payments and regulatory filings have deadlines that do not move. In this mission, a batch agent rehearses the monthly pension run and sees one job slowing down a full day ahead. It traces the cause to a storage rebalance and index growth, and the operations team fixes it in time. Every retiree is paid on time and the regulator gets its report.
narration.briefing: MetLife operates life, annuities and pensions in Chile. Retirees count on payments arriving on a known day. Regulators count on reports arriving on a known day. Either one missing becomes a reputational event.
narration.signal: Thirty hours before the bank cutoff, the batch agent compares tonight's rehearsal with history. One job in a chain of twenty two is running almost three times slower. The forecast says the payment file will miss the bank cutoff by three hours. Every job in the scheduler still shows green.
narration.traditional: In the traditional path, the scheduler shows green because jobs are running, just slowly. The bank cutoff is missed. Retirees call asking where their money is, the regulatory report is late, and the team spends the next week explaining and remediating.
narration.agentic: In the AgenticOps path, the correlation agent links the slowdown to a storage rebalance that overlaps the batch window, along with index growth on retiree records. It proposes moving the rebalance, rebuilding the indexes and adding parallel processing. With operations approval, the forecast finishes two hours early.
narration.outcome: The outcome is a promise kept to retirees and a clean record with regulators. Predictive operations protects the retirement business, which is one of the pillars of MetLife's strategy.

decision.prompt: The batch agent forecasts a 3-hour miss on the pension bank cutoff. Every job still shows green. What do you do?

options.label: Approve the agent remediation plan
options.detail: Move the storage rebalance, rebuild indexes, add parallel lanes.
options.feedback: Correct. Payments go out on time and the regulator receives the report.

options.label: Have someone watch the batch overnight
options.detail: Manual vigilance.
options.feedback: They see the slowdown at 2 AM with no time left to fix the cause. You end up with a partial miss.

options.label: Trust the scheduler
options.detail: Everything is green.
options.feedback: Green meant running, not on time. Retirees are paid late.

chain.signal: A batch job running slower than its historical baseline
chain.domain: Batch scheduling, storage, database and bank file transfer
chain.capability: Batch agent forecasting the deadline and remediating under approval

talkTrack: A deadline is a business outcome. Show how forecasting it changes the conversation.
Green does not mean on time. Agents compare runs against history and against the calendar.
This story is for the retirement business and compliance, not only infrastructure.
discovery: Which batch processes have hard external deadlines, like bank or regulator cutoffs?
How do you know early that a batch will finish late?
Who coordinates storage and infrastructure maintenance with business calendars?

In asset management, microseconds become millions.
